title: Staging to Prod: burst strategy & topology assessment
next_steps: Redwood to share dedicated capacity pricing and prewarm playbook (includes hot-pool sizes)
Maple to send 2-week traffic profile + model family and token estimates
Schedule a 48-hour PoC benchmark run with Redwood SE for week of 2026-10-26
action_items: Sofia: Share pricing and prewarm playbook by 2026-10-18
Liam: Draft recommended pool topology options and fallback policies by 2026-10-19
Daniel: Provide production RPS, percentiles, and current queueing behavior by 2026-10-20
summary: Discovery focused on moving Maple Analytics workloads from staging to production using Redwood Dedicated. Key topics: reserved GPU sizing, tenant isolation, hot-pool/prewarm strategies, autoscaling boundaries, cost/latency tradeoffs, security/compliance requirements, and a PoC benchmarking plan.
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm so excited to talk through the staging to prod move today, we've got about 40 minutes, is that still good?
[00:06] Priya Rao: yep that's perfect, ran into some late prep but all good.
[00:09] Daniel Kim: sorry slight background noise, i'll mute when i'm not talking.
[00:11] Liam Chen: great, Liam from Redwood here, i'll be the SE on the call. quick agenda: current stack, traffic shape, isolation needs, burst handling, and an ops playbook.
[00:20] Sara Liu: sounds good. quick context: Maple runs two main models for document summarization and a Q&A retrieval model. staging is on our k8s cluster with GPUs but we see flapping at peaks. our goal is consistent 95th pct latency under 350ms for user-facing flows.
[00:36] Priya Rao: to add, our QA team is happy with quality at current model sizes but production has 2x traffic spikes during reports release windows.
[00:45] Sofia Martinez: okay good, can you describe current burst patterns — is it short spikes (seconds/minutes) or long tail (hours)?
[00:52] Daniel Kim: mostly short spikes lasting 1-15 minutes, sometimes longer when a scheduled job kicks off, so a mix. on the cluster we see high queueing and OOM errors occasionally.
[01:03] Sofia Martinez: that aligns with what Dedicated with a hot pool is designed for — reserved nodes for baseline throughput and a hot-pool to cover short spikes with prewarmed models. question for Liam: recommended baseline pool for this workload?
[01:16] Liam Chen: based on their RPS goal and model sizes (they shared rough tokens), i'd start with a reserve equal to 60-70% of peak steady load and a small hot pool sized to cover 20-30% additional burst with quick spin-up for larger surges. we can do a bench to tune. note: hot-pool prewarm time depends on model (LLama variants vs OPT, etc.) and quantization.
[01:38] Priya Rao: models are Llama2-13B fine-tuned and a DistilT5 variant for summarization. we use FP16 in staging.
[01:46] Liam Chen: fp16 reduces warm times vs jpq quant but still need KV cache priming. for Llama2-13B expect a few seconds to warm if cold, hot-pool avoids that.
[01:55] Sara Liu: can dedicated fall back to Redwood hosted if we exhaust reserved capacity?
[01:59] Sofia Martinez: yes, smart routing policies can failover to hosted variants in the same region; that is a common safety net. we usually recommend an explicit fallback SLA/priority so critical requests can route to hosted with a slightly cheaper model or increased tail latency tolerance.
[02:13] Daniel Kim: how about isolation — do we need VPC/private plane? our security team requires no cross-tenant memory leaks and customer data never leaves our VPC.
[02:22] Liam Chen: Redwood Private is an option if you need customer-managed networking or on-prem. Dedicated offers strong tenant fencing at the node level, NVSwitch isolation patterns, and we can support VPC peering or private endpoints. if KMS integration is needed for keys, we support bring-your-own KMS.
[02:37] Priya Rao: SOC 2 and audit logs are required. do you have an SOC 2 cert for Dedicated?
[02:42] Sofia Martinez: we have SOC 2 for the control plane and options for audit logging retention. i'll share our security deck link and compliance summary after this call.
[02:51] Sara Liu: great. pricing — curious how prewarm/hot-pool is charged; we want predictable unit economics.
[02:57] Sofia Martinez: reserved nodes are a flat monthly commit; hot-pools are usually billed as per-minute when active on top of baseline. we also provide guidance for batching/kv cache to reduce per-token costs. i'll send a model pricing sheet.
[03:12] Priya Rao: on batching — we have a lot of deterministic short prompts, so batching isn't as effective for latency sensitive paths.
[03:20] Liam Chen: understood; then prefix KV caching and request-level cache can help reduce tokens without affecting latency. also consider quantization profiles for cost saving if quality tolerates.
[03:30] Daniel Kim: how do we detect bursts? our monitoring currently just alerts on queue length.
[03:36] Liam Chen: common pattern: monitor request rate + queue length + drop in tail throughput; define a surge rule that triggers hot-pool prewarm and temporary routing changes. Redwood can run prewarm based on predictive windows too — e.g., known report times.
[03:49] Sofia Martinez: do you have planned release windows?
[03:51] Priya Rao: yes, monthly reports every 1st of month cause 3-5x spike for 7-10 minutes. we could schedule prewarm for those windows.
[03:58] Sofia Martinez: perfect use-case for scheduled hot-pool prewarming.
[04:01] Sara Liu: what's the rollback story if a model update degrades latency/quality?
[04:04] Liam Chen: Redwood supports pinned model versions and can do canary rollouts; traffic split and automatic fallback to previous variant if error rate or latency regresses. we also integrate with your eval sets to gate rollouts.
[04:16] Daniel Kim: curious about network egress and data residency — our legal team asks where logs go and if we can turn off extraction for certain fields.
[04:24] Sofia Martinez: you can configure masking and opt-out for logs; audit logs can be sent to your SIEM if desired. Redwood Private gives you full control over where telemetry is stored.
[04:34] Priya Rao: any known gotchas moving from FP16 in staging to a quantized setup in Dedicated?
[04:39] Liam Chen: yes, quantization can change latency/quality tradeoffs; we recommend a small eval sweep. sometimes KV cache behavior and tokenization differences cause small regressions. we surface those with our Optimize tool.
[04:52] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[04:54] Sofia Martinez: quick question on metrics — what's your SLO window? 95th at 350ms was mentioned, any error budget?
[04:59] Sara Liu: we'd like under 350ms 95th for UI calls, but background jobs can be relaxed to 2s. error budget TBD but aiming for 99.5% availability for inference.
[05:12] Liam Chen: that will shape baseline sizing and fallback tolerance — to hit 95th 350ms we need tight batching and small queueing. for Dedicated we can prioritize latency through node sizing and scheduling policies.
[05:24] Priya Rao: about autoscaling — do you do instant scale up or gradual? bursts are so short i'm worried about spin-up latencies.
[05:31] Liam Chen: autoscaling on Dedicated can be configured for fast scale by keeping a warm pool plus immediate prewarm. true instant (sub-second) isn't realistic for large models, so warm/hot pools are the pattern.
[05:42] Daniel Kim: do you support GPU partitioning or multi-tenant inference on a single GPU? we prefer strict tenant isolation.
[05:49] Liam Chen: we don't recommend multi-tenant GPU sharing for production if isolation is required — we offer single-tenant reservations or strict containerized fencing. there are approaches for fractional GPUs but with tradeoffs in observability and tail latency.
[06:02] Sofia Martinez: we should talk about a pilot — a 48-hour benchmark where Redwood runs a simulated production traffic pattern with your model and the two fallback options: hot-pool only, and hot-pool + hosted fallback.
[06:14] Priya Rao: that'd be ideal. what instrumentation do you need?
[06:17] Liam Chen: request traces, token counts, RPS by route, and a sample of payload sizes. Daniel can provide RPS histogram and a small prompt corpus.
[06:25] Daniel Kim: yeah we can provide that; i'll export last 30 days of traffic shape.
[06:29] Sara Liu: timeline — we want to be in production before end of Q4. is that feasible?
[06:33] Sofia Martinez: feasible if pilot happens in the next two weeks and security/compliance review moves quickly. we'll fast-track Dedicated onboarding for pilots.
[06:42] Priya Rao: what about failover behavior at the edge — do requests queue then spill over?
[06:46] Liam Chen: typical pattern: short queue then trigger prewarm; if queue exceeds threshold and we've hit capacity the routing policy can spill to hosted or throttle non-critical requests. it's configurable per-route.
[06:58] Speaker 2: that's helpful.
[07:00] Sofia Martinez: question for Daniel — what's your current peak GPU utilization and typical concurrency per GPU?
[07:06] Daniel Kim: right now peaks hit 95% across a handful of nodes, concurrency per GPU varies but overall utilization is high so we need more headroom.
[07:13] Liam Chen: that supports the 60-70% baseline reserve idea. also consider isolating high-priority tenants onto dedicated node pools.
[07:21] Priya Rao: we have internal tiers: UI latency-critical, API batch, and nightly ingest. can those be mapped to different pools?
[07:27] Liam Chen: yes, multi-pool strategy recommended: small low-latency pool for UI, larger cost-optimized pool for background, plus a hot pool bridging them.
[07:36] Sara Liu: can we do rate-limited fallback for background jobs to avoid paying hosted costs?
[07:40] Sofia Martinez: absolutely, routing can be prioritized so background jobs get deprioritized or rate-limited to save cost.
[07:47] Daniel Kim: how do we measure cost impact of different prewarm sizes?
[07:51] Liam Chen: Redwood Optimize can simulate cost per token under different hot-pool sizes and batching; we can run a quick cost sensitivity analysis as part of the pilot.
[08:02] Priya Rao: good. any limits on the number of reserved pools per account?
[08:06] Sofia Martinez: not practically — we can provision multiple pools with governance rules. we'll share a recommended topology doc.
[08:12] Sara Liu: one more on security — if we use private deployment, is there still a control plane on Redwood side?
[08:18] Liam Chen: the Private deployment can be customer-controlled for inference plane while control plane interactions can be via a private channel; we also have an air-gap option but that tends to be more lead time.
[08:29] Priya Rao: okay let's recap next steps.
[08:31] Sofia Martinez: recap: Redwood sends pricing, prewarm/hot-pool playbook, and recommended pool topology. Maple sends traffic histogram, sample prompts, and SLOs. schedule the 48-hour PoC the week of 10/26. action items captured in the notes.
[08:45] Daniel Kim: confirmed.
[08:47] Sara Liu: i'm cc'ing security on the follow-up thread.
[08:50] Liam Chen: i'll prepare the benchmark harness and a default config for the PoC.
[08:55] Priya Rao: thanks everyone. that was productive.
[08:58] Sofia Martinez: thanks all — we'll follow up with links and the pricing doc. end of call.
[09:03] (call ends)
